title: Magic Link (Passwordless Email Login)
subtitle: Request a link by email, click a single-use time-limited token, and a POST consumes it to establish a normal session cookie. Step through it and watch the token move from URL to session.

steps.label: Enter email on login page
steps.lede: The user provides only an email address — no password. The app will email a link that proves control of the mailbox.
steps.devtools: Open DevTools (F12) → Network, enable Preserve log so the redirect chain survives navigation. Filter on Fetch/XHR + Doc.

steps.label: POST /auth/magic-link (email only)
steps.lede: The browser posts the email. The server generates a high-entropy token, stores only its hash with a short TTL and single-use flag, and emails the link.

resp.json: { "message": "If an account exists, check your email." }

steps.devtools: In Payload confirm only an email is sent — no password. The 200 response is a generic "check your email" that is identical whether or not the account exists: that is enumeration protection. Nothing sensitive is returned here.

steps.label: Click link in email
steps.lede: The user opens the emailed link, possibly on a different device than the one that requested it. The token lives in the URL query string.
steps.devtools: The session lands on whichever device clicks the link, not necessarily the one that made the request. Because the token is in a URL, it can leak via history, Referer, and logs — hence single-use + short TTL.

steps.label: GET /auth/verify?token=… (does NOT consume)
steps.lede: The link opens a confirmation page. By design this GET does not consume the token, so mail scanners and link-preview bots that pre-fetch the URL cannot burn it.
steps.devtools: Open the row's Query String Parameters to read token=ml_SYNTHETIC_…. This GET only renders the confirm page — the token is consumed by the follow-up POST, which defeats prefetching bots.

steps.label: POST /auth/verify (consume token)
steps.lede: Clicking Confirm posts the token. The server hashes it, atomically looks-up-and-consumes it (checking expiry and single-use), then issues a rotated session cookie. From here it is an ordinary session.

headers: sid=s%3AsynthSESSION0a1b2c3d4e5f6071; Path=/; Max-Age=1800; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

jwt.title: Set-Cookie attributes
payload: Opaque server-side session reference — the magic link is now spent

steps.devtools: In Response Headers see Set-Cookie: sid=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax and the 303 to /dashboard. Replaying this POST should fail (a 4xx with no new Set-Cookie) — the token is single-use.

steps.label: Subsequent requests replay Cookie
steps.lede: The magic link is gone; from here the browser replays Cookie: sid=… on every request, exactly like classic session-cookie auth.
steps.devtools: In Request Headers the browser now attaches Cookie: sid=… automatically. The one-time token has been exchanged for a durable server-side session — see the session-cookie flow for how that cookie behaves from here.
